The intended handling of zero-length (unavailable-day) overrides is therefore dead code, and only the following instant comparisons apply. Use `.isSame(...)` instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: using the `===` operator to compare `dayjs` objects, which compares object references and always returns false instead of comparing the dates. Both suggest using the `.isSame()` method instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Date override short-circuits before the busy check, so already-booked slots are reported available

In `checkIfIsAvailable`, once a slot falls inside a date override the function returns `true` at line 134, before the `busy.every(...)` check at the end of the function. A date override is only meant to replace the working-hours check; the host's `busy` entries (Cal bookings plus connected-calendar events) must still make the slot unavailable. Because personal events mark every user as `isFixed`, and this helper is used for both the fixed-host filter and the loose-host filter, any host with a date override will be shown as available during a time they are already booked, producing bookable slots that double-book the host. The new tests place no booking on the override day, so this is not caught.

`workingHours.find` rejects a slot when any same-day range does not contain it and never rejects a non-working day

The block rejects the slot whenever `workingHours.find(...)` returns a range whose `days` include the weekday and whose bounds do not contain the slot. This has two wrong consequences: (a) if a host has more than one availability range on the same weekday (the `Availability` model/API permits multiple rows for a date), a slot inside range 2 is still rejected because it is outside range 1; (b) if no range exists for that weekday at all (the host does not work that day), nothing matches and the slot is accepted, so a round-robin event still offers slots on days the fixed host is unavailable. The correct test is 'reject unless some range covers the slot', e.g. `workingHours.some(w => w.days.includes(day) && start >= w.startTime && end <= w.endTime)`.

Multiple date overrides on the same day: first non-matching override marks the slot unavailable

`dateOverrides.find(...)` stops as soon as the callback returns `true`, and the callback returns `true` when the override is on the slot's day but the slot is outside that override's range. If a user has two overrides on the same date (e.g. 10:00-11:00 and 14:00-15:00, which the `Availability` table permits), a slot inside the second range is reported as unavailable because it is outside the first. The day should be classified with `some()` - is the slot covered by at least one override on that date - before deciding availability.

Override day match mixes local and UTC dates and only looks at the override start

`dayjs(date.start)` is a Dayjs in the server's local timezone, while `slotStartTime` was created with `.utc()`, so the `format("YYYY MM DD")` comparison compares a local date against a UTC date. On servers not running in UTC (and near day boundaries on any server) the override is attached to the wrong date. In addition, the match uses only the converted `start` instant, so an override whose real-UTC window crosses midnight (typical for early-morning overrides in positive-offset organizer timezones, e.g. 05:00-06:30 Asia/Kolkata) is not recognized for the slots after UTC midnight; those slots then fall through to the working-hours check and are wrongly dropped. Build the override window with `dayjs.utc(...)` and test whether the slot overlaps that window instead of string-comparing dates.

No coverage for the fixed-host round-robin fix or for a booking inside a date override

The added test only asserts the UTC output of `getSlots` for a second invitee timezone. All asserted slots (08:30-12:30 UTC) also lie inside the fixture's normal working hours (04:00-12:30 UTC), so the assertions still pass if the new date-override/working-hours logic in `checkIfIsAvailable` is removed entirely - the test does not exercise the router change. The PR's headline fix (a round-robin event whose fixed host has a date override) has no test, and no test puts an existing booking inside the override window, so the busy-check bypass in `checkIfIsAvailable` is not detected.

Test comment gives the wrong reason for the expected result

The comment `// it should return the same as this is the utc time` is misleading: the invitee gets the same UTC slots in both cases because the slots are absolute instants and the override is anchored to the organizer's timezone, not because 'this is the utc time'. As written it suggests the second assertion is trivially true, whereas it is precisely the assertion that fails with the old `getUTCHours()` logic (which would yield 08:00/09:00/10:00/11:00 UTC for Asia/Dhaka). The comment should explain that the override must represent the same absolute time regardless of the viewer's timezone.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry count uses a stale read-modify-write instead of an atomic increment

Both failure paths write `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` using the value fetched once before the loop. true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Adding order() as an abstract method breaks existing third-party CryptoProvider implementations

CryptoProvider is a public interface in keycloak-common that external/extension code implements (custom FIPS variants, etc.). Adding `int order();` as a non-default abstract method is a source- and binary-incompatible change: existing implementations will no longer compile, and prebuilt implementations will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when CryptoIntegration.detectProvider sorts by CryptoProvider::order. Since the interface already uses default methods (getSupportedKeyStoreTypes, getSupportedRsaKeySizes), order() should be declared `default int order() { return 0; }` so existing providers keep working and get a sane default priority.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same backward-compatibility issue: adding abstract order() to CryptoProvider breaks existing implementations. The candidate adds details about compilation and runtime failures and proposes a default method.

false_positives.candidate:
Removing the multi-provider failure and relying on order() allows non-deterministic/unsafe provider selection

Before this change, loading more than one CryptoProvider threw an IllegalStateException, which was a deliberate fail-fast guard against ambiguous crypto configuration. The code now silently keeps the highest-order provider and only debug-logs the others. However DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order() == 200 (see the other files in this PR), so when two of them are on the classpath (for example a FIPS deployment that also pulls in keycloak-crypto-default) the sort leaves their relative order unchanged and the winner is the ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order, which is undefined. The result is that a FIPS deployment can silently select the non-FIPS DefaultCryptoProvider instead of failing, i.e. it silently weakens crypto/compliance guarantee. Equal orders should be detected and rejected (or at minimum given distinct, guaranteed values) rather than resolved by an arbitrary tie-break.

Test uses a default (P-256) key for all ES256/ES384/ES512, so ES384/ES512 are not exercised realistically

The key pair is generated with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, which on standard JDKs defaults to a P-256 key regardless of the algorithm under test. ES384 and ES512 are still run over this P-256 key, so the produced r/s values are only 32 bytes and `integerToBytes(..., len)` just pads them to 48/66 bytes; the real P-384/P-521 cases (where r/s can be 48/66 bytes with leading high bits) are never tested. The round-trip assertion still passes, so the test gives a false sense that the 96- and 132-byte signature paths are validated. Generate a curve-specific key (e.g. `ECGenParameterSpec("secp384r1"/"secp521r1")`) per algorithm.

No test covers the new multi-provider ordering/selection logic

The core behavioral change of this PR is that detectProvider now sorts providers by order() and picks the highest instead of failing on multiple providers, but there is no test asserting which provider is selected when several are present, nor that the ignored providers are logged. The only added test (ECDSAAlgorithmTest) instantiates AuthzClientCryptoProvider directly and never goes through CryptoIntegration. A test with two registered providers of different order (and ideally an equal-order case) would protect this logic from regressions.

OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint routes optimized_pagination=true requests to OptimizedCursorPaginator with order_by="-datetime", so self.key is "datetime". true_positives.matched_candidate:
Concurrent builds for the same index key are no longer serialized

BuildIndex used to hold cacheMu for the entire build; now it only locks around the final map write. Two goroutines can call BuildIndex for the same NamespacedResource at the same time because getOrCreateIndex has no per-key lock and both Search and watch-event handling can call it. For file-backed indexes both call bleve.New on the same directory, which can fail or corrupt the index; for memory indexes they create two separate indexes, the last one wins in the cache, and callers may keep using a different instance. Add a per-key mutex or singleflight and re-check the cache under it before building.

TotalDocs iterates b.cache with no cacheMu, while BuildIndex now writes to the same map under cacheMu. The new log line in searchSupport.init (resource/search.go:216) calls TotalDocs after starting the watch goroutine, so an event can trigger getOrCreateIndex/BuildIndex and mutate the map while TotalDocs iterates, causing a fatal concurrent map iteration and map write. false_positives.candidate:
init shares one err variable across errgroup workers

Each errgroup goroutine assigns to the outer err via `_, _, err = s.build(...)` and also increments totalBatchesIndexed without synchronization. With multiple workers these are data races; one successful build can overwrite another build's error before it is returned, so errgroup.Wait may see nil and startup can continue with a missing index. Use local per-goroutine error variables (`_, _, buildErr := s.build(...); return buildErr`) and an atomic or mutex-protected counter.

Watch loop dereferences nil when the event channel is closed

The goroutine receives from events without checking the closed-channel ok value, then passes nil to handleEvent, which dereferences evt.Type. The SQL backend closes its WatchWriteEvents channel when the backend is stopped (defer close(stream) in sql/backend.go:572), so stopping a search-enabled server will panic the process. Receive with `v, ok := <-events` and return when !ok, and tie the watcher to a cancelable lifecycle context. The same closed-channel pattern exists in server.initWatcher.

Constructor leaks initialized resources when Init fails

NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) and returns nil on failure, but never calls s.cancel() or lifecycle.Stop. If lifecycle.Init and search.init succeeded and a later step such as initWatcher fails, the search watch goroutine and open DB resources are left running with a context that is never canceled. Clean up on the error path before returning.

false_positives.candidate:
Uses queue.Queue.shutdown/queue.ShutDown, which require Python 3.13+

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown` calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` and the worker catches `queue.ShutDown`. Both APIs were added in Python 3.13. On older supported runtimes the shutdown path raises AttributeError for every queue and workers blocked in `get()` are never released; the worker exception handler also cannot resolve `queue.ShutDown`, so an unexpected processing exception can kill the worker thread. This makes the new consumer unable to shut down correctly unless the whole repository is already on Python 3.13.

Broad submit exception handler commits offsets for messages that were never enqueued

If `grouping_fn(result)` raises, or if `queue_pool.submit` fails (for example `work_queue.put` raises `ShutDown` during shutdown), the `except Exception` block calls `add_offset` plus `complete_offset` for the message. The commit thread then sees the offset as complete and commits past it even though the message was never processed or even queued. Only an intentional decode failure returning `None` should be skipped; unexpected failures must propagate, retry, or go to a DLQ rather than silently advancing the Kafka offset.

Worker marks an offset complete even when result processing raised

`OrderedQueueWorker.run` catches `Exception` from `result_processor`, logs it, and then unconditionally calls `complete_offset` in `finally`. Any exception that escapes processing (a bug, tracing failure, unexpected DB error, etc.) therefore makes the offset committable and permanently skips that message. This contradicts the class contract that offsets are only committed after successful processing and turns transient failures into silent data loss.

Commit callback is invoked from a background thread concurrently with the stream processor

`_commit_loop` runs on its own thread and calls the arroyo `Commit` callback, which ultimately commits the Kafka consumer used by the main `StreamProcessor` polling thread. The Confluent Kafka consumer and arroyo commit path are not thread-safe, and existing strategies only call `commit` from the processing thread. This can race with `poll`/rebalance and cause undefined behavior, failed commits, or duplicate processing. Commit requests should be handed back to the processing thread or otherwise serialized.

Work queues are unbounded, so the strategy has no backpressure

`queue.Queue()` is created with the default `maxsize=0`, so `put()` never blocks. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` continues accepting messages as fast as Kafka delivers them even if one or more queues cannot keep up; each queued `WorkItem` retains both the decoded result and the full original `Message`. A single slow subscription can therefore grow memory without bound and eventually OOM the consumer. The class docstring claiming `Natural backpressure when queues fill up` is false unless a bounded queue and blocking submission are added.

Shutdown stops workers before draining queued work

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets every worker's `shutdown` flag before shutting down the queues. Workers check that flag only at the top of the loop, so a worker that is processing an item exits immediately afterwards even if more items remain in its queue. The existing `wait_until_empty` helper is never used. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close`/`join` therefore can abandon messages that were already accepted by `submit`, causing avoidable reprocessing on restart and making the `graceful shutdown` behavior misleading. Shutdown should stop accepting new work, drain queued and in-flight items, and only then stop workers.

Error-handling test asserts no commit even though failed offsets are marked complete

The test patches `result_processor.__call__` to raise for offset 100 and succeed for offset 101. In the implementation, the worker catches the exception and `finally` calls `complete_offset`, so both offsets become committable and the commit loop will normally commit past offset 100. The assertion `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` can only pass if the 1-second commit thread happens not to run during the 0.2-second sleep, so the test is timing-dependent and also does not encode the intended error semantics. It should explicitly define whether failed messages are retried, sent to a DLQ, or committed, and assert that contract deterministically.

Stats test races with live queue workers

`test_stats_reporting` submits ten items to a live pool and immediately asserts `stats['total_items'] > 0`. The three worker threads can dequeue and process all ten items before `get_stats()` is called, making `total_items` zero and causing an intermittent failure. The test should synchronize with the workers (for example by pausing them or using a barrier) instead of assuming queue depth remains non-zero after submission.

false_positives.candidate:
Switching span-buffer keys from sets to sorted sets breaks existing Redis data and rolling deploys

The buffer still uses the existing `span-buf:s:...` key namespace, but now writes with `zadd` and reads with `zscan`/`zcard`. Any keys created by the previous version are Redis sets, not sorted sets. During an upgrade or rolling deploy, processing a batch that touches an existing set key raises a Redis `WRONGTYPE` error at this `p.zadd` or in `add-buffer.lua`; batches then fail and in-flight segments can be lost until those keys expire. The key type change needs a new key namespace/version or an explicit drain/migration before deployment.

max_segment_spans is no longer enforced; eviction cap is hardcoded in Lua

The previous `_load_segment_data` check that skipped a segment once it exceeded `self.max_segment_spans` was removed and is not replaced on the Python side. The only cap is now the literal `1000` in `add-buffer.lua`, so `SpansBuffer(max_segment_spans=...)` has no effect, and deployments that configured a different limit silently keep/evict up to 1000 spans without the old `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric. Either pass the configurable limit into the Lua path or remove the parameter and update callers/tests.

Redirect depth limit was silently reduced from 10000 to 1000

The loop resolving parent redirects now stops after 1000 hops. For a segment tree deeper than 1000, the script writes a redirect to that truncated ancestor and merges spans into a non-root buffer, causing incorrectly split/merged segments. The previous limit was 10000 and had an explanatory comment; this behavior change is unrelated to eviction and has no covering test.

No test covers the new zset eviction behavior

The changed tests only add the required `end_timestamp_precise` argument to existing `Span` constructions. They never ingest more than 1000 spans into a segment or assert which spans are evicted, so the new `zpopmin` cap, eviction ordering, and root-span retention are untested. Add a case with more than 1000 spans and explicitly verify the cap and evicted members.

The result is serialized, repeated I/O for N concurrent requests instead of a single load, and each late arrival overwrites the cache written by the previous one. A double-checked-locking pattern (re-test `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` immediately after `Lock()` and return the cached value) is needed to avoid the thundering-herd recompute.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are only loaded in controllers, so fallbacks fail in mailers/background jobs

The accelerator's `translate` only lazy-loads the active locale (`load_locale(config.locale)` on line 68); it never loads the fallback locales returned by `I18n.fallbacks[locale]`. The only place that force-loads the fallback chain is `ApplicationController#set_locale` (app/controllers/application_controller.rb:159 → `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!`). Any translation performed outside an HTTP request — ActionMailer, Sidekiq/background workers, rake tasks, console — never runs `set_locale`, so `:en` (and the site default) yml is not loaded. When a key is missing in the user's locale the Fallbacks backend tries `:en`, finds no loaded data, and the caller gets a "translation missing" string instead of the English fallback. This defeats the stated 'server-side fallbacks' goal for exactly the server-side paths (emails etc.) that need it most. The fallback locales should be loaded inside the translate/locale-loading path rather than only from the controller.

Fallback chain does a DB-backed SiteSetting lookup on every translation

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` builds its result from `SiteSetting.default_locale`, which is a runtime site setting rather than a boot-time constant. `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` calls `I18n.fallbacks[locale]` for essentially every `I18n.t` lookup (the accelerator routes all translation through the backend), so this now performs a `SiteSetting.default_locale` read (and allocates a fresh array) on the hot translation path for every request. In addition to the overhead, it makes translation depend on `SiteSetting` being initialized: in contexts without a ready DB/settings (boot, `rake db:migrate`, `rake assets:precompile`, or if the setting is nil so `.to_sym` raises NoMethodError) any `I18n.t` call can raise instead of returning a translation. The fallback list should be computed once/memoized with a safe hard-coded default instead of reading SiteSetting per lookup.

No tests for the new fallback behavior

This PR changes global i18n behavior (enables Fallbacks in every environment, replaces the default fallbacks object, and adds an `ensure_loaded!` hook) but adds no specs. There is no coverage that a key missing in a non-English locale resolves to the site default and then to English, that `ensure_loaded!` actually loads the fallback locales' yml, or that a missing key still raises/returns the expected result. Given this touches translation resolution for all requests and is easy to regress, at least a request spec exercising a missing translation in a non-English locale and a unit test for `FallbackLocaleList#[]`/`ensure_loaded!` should be added.

Translation cache key omits fallback/default locale, so changing default_locale yields stale fallback text

The LRU cache key is `"#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}"`, which only captures the requested locale. With fallbacks now resolving through `SiteSetting.default_locale`, the *value* stored for a given locale can change when an admin changes the default locale, but the key does not, so previously cached fallback-resolved strings keep being served until `I18n.reload!` happens to be called. For locales whose own translations are incomplete, this means users continue to see text from the old default-locale fallback after the setting is changed. The cache key (or a `reload!` on default_locale change) should account for the fallback chain.

The replacement uses `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 50%))`, changing the light-theme color from 30% to 50% and using 50% from `$secondary` in dark theme instead of the expected 70%. This makes the member name lighter than before and inconsistent with the same selector on desktop. It should be `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 70%))`.

Category badge-notification still uses $primary in dark themes

The PR converts the muted topic-list colors in this file to `dark-light-choose`, but `.topic-list.categories .category .badge-notification` still uses `color: scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%)`. Since `$primary` is light in dark themes, this badge count is lightened further instead of being derived from `$secondary`, so the original dark-theme contrast issue remains for category badge notifications. It should be converted like the surrounding rules, e.g. `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 50%))`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the next action, capping the next offset at user_count can produce an empty page (e.g., total equal to limit results in offset == total, showing 2/2 with no members). This can cause confusing UX on the last page.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
totalPages is off by one when user_count is a multiple of limit

totalPages is computed as Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1. When user_count is an exact multiple of limit (e.g. 50 members and limit 50) this returns 2 instead of 1. The template then renders '1/2', and because showingLast compares currentPage to this wrong totalPages, the 'next' link is not disabled on what is really the last page. Clicking next advances offset to user_count, findMembers requests that offset, the server returns an empty page, and the user is left looking at an empty member list. Use Math.ceil(user_count / limit) (or Math.floor((user_count - 1) / limit) + 1).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the pagination bug that allows advancing to offset == user_count, producing an empty last page when the total is an exact multiple of the limit. The candidate explains how the off-by-one page count enables this same confusing UX.

true_positives.golden_comment: The remove_member test uses xhr :put to call the remove_member action, but the route defines delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member' requiring DELETE method.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
remove_member test uses PUT although the route is DELETE

The 'cannot remove members from automatic groups' example issues xhr :put, :remove_member, but config/routes.rb maps remove_member to DELETE. Controller specs bypass routing, so the test passes even though it never exercises the real verb/route the browser uses; a mismatch between the configured route and the action would go undetected. Issue :delete here to match the actual route (the 'is able to remove a member' example already uses :delete).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same HTTP verb mismatch: the remove_member test uses xhr :put, while the route requires DELETE. The candidate adds context and recommends the corresponding fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `totalPages` calculation using `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` produces an extra page when `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`, leading to incorrect pagination. For example, with 100 users and a limit of 50, it reports 3 pages instead of 2, allowing navigation to an empty page.

The template then renders '1/2', and because showingLast compares currentPage to this wrong totalPages, the 'next' link is not disabled on what is really the last page. Clicking next advances offset to user_count, findMembers requests that offset, the server returns an empty page, and the user is left looking at an empty member list. true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same off-by-one bug in Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1 when user_count is an exact multiple of limit, which overstates totalPages and permits navigation to an empty page.

false_positives.candidate:
remove_member deletes the join row directly and leaves groups.user_count stale

remove_member removes the membership with group.users.delete(user_id) followed by group.save, instead of using the Group#remove path. The groups.user_count column is a denormalized counter (the .index spec shows it is stored and populated by group.add). Deleting the join record directly bypasses whatever keeps that counter in sync (Group#remove and/or a counter cache / GroupUser callbacks, which delete_all does not trigger), so after removing a member the stored user_count remains too high. The admin groups list and the group header render that stored count, so they will report a wrong member total until it is recomputed. Use Group#remove (or recompute user_count) and cover it with a spec asserting user_count — the current spec only asserts users.count.

Group members endpoint now silently truncates to 50 with no pagination on the public page

members now always paginates: limit defaults to 50 and the previous behavior (all members for non-automatic groups, up to 200 for automatic groups) is gone. The public group members page (app/assets/javascripts/discourse/templates/group/members.hbs) was not given pagination controls and only iterates `members`, so any group with more than 50 members now silently shows just the first 50 with no way to load the rest. In addition the response changed from a bare array to {members, meta}, which breaks any client of the public /groups/:id/members.json route that still expects an array. Either add pagination to that template or keep returning the full list for this endpoint.

add_members splits usernames without stripping whitespace

add_members does usernames.split(",") and passes each element straight to User.find_by_username without stripping. If the client ever submits a space-separated list such as "alice, bob", the lookup for " bob" fails and that user is silently not added (the old Group#usernames= setter stripped entries). Strip each element and drop blanks before lookup.

Unbounded limit parameter on the public members endpoint

members reads the caller-supplied limit with no upper bound: (params[:limit] || 50).to_i. This is a public (non-admin) route, so a request with limit=1000000 forces the entire membership set to be loaded and serialized in one response. Clamp limit to a sane maximum (e.g. the page size) before applying it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email statistics are updated during validation, causing duplicate and racy increments

`should_block?` increments `match_count` and saves the record every time it is called, but it is called from `EmailValidator`, so every validation pass mutates the database. In `UsersController#create` the code calls `user.valid?` and then `user.save`, which re-runs validations, so one blocked signup attempt increments `match_count` at least twice; every additional `valid?` call increments it again. The `match_count += 1`/`save` sequence is also a non-atomic read-modify-write, so concurrent attempts can lose increments. Move the statistics update out of the validation path or use an atomic update, and avoid validating the same user twice in the controller.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying issue: a blocked-email check mutates statistics during a read/validation operation, creating concurrency risks. The candidate adds specific consequences such as duplicate increments and lost updates, which are consistent with the golden concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Domain whitelist regex is unanchored and can be bypassed

The restriction regex is built as `@(#{domains})` with no end anchor. If `email_domains_whitelist` is `example.com`, the address `user@example.com.attacker.tld` matches because the string contains `@example.com`, even though the actual domain is under `attacker.tld`. Since this validator is the only server-side domain check, an attacker controlling `attacker.tld` can satisfy a whitelist they should not satisfy; blacklist matching can also produce false positives. Anchor the domain pattern at the end (and add specs covering lookalike domains).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same improperly anchored @(#{domains}) regex as allowing unintended domains to satisfy the whitelist. Although their example domains differ, the underlying boundary-matching vulnerability is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email matching is case- and whitespace-sensitive, allowing bypass

`BlockedEmail.should_block?` looks up the address with an exact `where(email: email)` match, and `BlockedEmail` does not normalize email on write; the migration's unique index on `email` also does not enforce case-insensitive uniqueness. The User model/controller do not downcase or strip `params[:email]` before validation, so an address blocked as `bad@spam.com` is not matched when submitted as `Bad@Spam.com` or with surrounding whitespace, and the account can still be created. Normalize email on insert and lookup (e.g. `strip.downcase`), make uniqueness/index case-insensitive, and add a regression spec for mixed-case input.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same case-sensitive email lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block? that lets mixed-case variants of blocked addresses bypass the block. The candidate adds whitespace and normalization concerns without changing the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
align-items mixin omits -moz-box-align and emits an invalid -ms property

`flexbox()` emits `display: -moz-box`, but `align-items()` never emits the corresponding `-moz-box-align`; it also emits `-ms-align-items`, which is not a real CSS property. In an old Firefox that falls back to `-moz-box`, requested alignment (`center` in the header and `.small-action`, `baseline` in badges) will not apply, and the non-existent `-ms-align-items` declaration is dead code. Add `-moz-box-align: $alignment` and remove `-ms-align-items`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies -ms-align-items as a nonexistent CSS property, matching the golden issue. Although it also flags missing Firefox support and does not name -ms-flex-align as the replacement, it identifies the same underlying bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy order properties need +1 to match standard order semantics

The new `order($val)` mixin passes the standard zero-based `order` value directly to `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` and `-moz-box-ordinal-group`. Those legacy flexbox properties are one-based and default to 1, while modern `order` defaults to 0. Calls such as `order(0)` or `order(1)` will place items differently in the old `-webkit-box`/`-moz-box` fallback than in modern flex. Emit `$val + 1` for the legacy properties while keeping `$val` for `-ms-flex-order`, `-webkit-order`, and `order`. The current 2/3 calls happen to preserve their relative order, but the reusable mixin is incorrect for common values.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: passing zero-based order values directly to the one-based -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group properties, causing incorrect legacy-browser layout, particularly when $val is 0.

false_positives.candidate:
Flex container ignores the small-action button's float, losing right alignment

Making `.small-action` a flex container turns its direct children into flex items. The existing `button { float: right; }` at line 309 is therefore ignored, and the button has no auto margin or other flex rule that allocates the remaining space. The action/undo button will render immediately after `.small-action-desc` instead of at the right edge of the row. Add `margin-left: auto` to the button or otherwise distribute the free space explicitly.

Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
website_name bypasses TL0 untrusted-field filtering and is always serialized

ActiveModel::Serializer only consults `include_<attribute>?` predicates. The new guard is named `include_website_name` (without the question mark), and `website_name` is not added to `untrusted_attributes`. Consequently every user JSON now contains `website_name`, even for a TL0 user viewed anonymously, for whom the existing `website` attribute is intentionally suppressed by `untrusted_attributes :website`. The profile template then renders that field, leaking the host/path of a website that was deliberately hidden. Rename the guard to `include_website_name?` and apply at least the same `scope.restrict_user_fields?`/presence gate as `website`, or add `website_name` to `untrusted_attributes`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same missing '?' suffix on include_website_name and its effect on conditional serialization. It does not mention the string-literal mutation concern, but directly matches the golden comment's primary issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Host comparison treats unrelated hosts under public suffixes as the same domain

The equal-label branch strips only the first label before comparing hosts. For an instance host such as `other.co.uk` and a user website of `example.co.uk`, both have three labels and both reduce to `co.uk`, so the code treats them as the same domain and returns `example.co.uk/path`. These are unrelated registrable domains (the same problem occurs for `alice.github.io` versus `bob.github.io`). The path should only be appended when the hosts actually belong to the same registrable domain, which requires public-suffix-aware comparison or a narrower exact/parent check rather than comparing `split('.')[1..-1]`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Imported-from footer interpolates an untrusted URL into raw HTML

`url` comes from an RSS/Atom item and is only checked with a loose `^https?://` regex. It is interpolated directly into `href='#{url}'` and appended to the raw HTML body. A URL containing a single quote and attribute text, such as `http://host/'onmouseover='alert(1)`, can produce an extra event-handler attribute in the generated anchor. Because the post is stored as raw HTML, this is another stored XSS vector. Escape the URL with `ERB::Util.html_escape` or build the link with `link_to` and sanitize the final HTML.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same XSS vulnerability caused by interpolating an unescaped URL into generated HTML. It does not mention the nil contents NoMethodError, but it directly matches the golden comment's XSS concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Invalid `end if` makes the best view fail to compile

`<%- end if %>` is not valid Ruby: it closes the `if` and then starts an `if` modifier with no condition. Rendering the `best` action after a topic has been found will raise a template syntax error, so existing embeds return 500 instead of displaying the topic. It should be `<%- end %>`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the invalid ERB closing statement `end if`, which causes a template syntax error, and specify replacing it with `end`.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Referer value is interpolated into JavaScript without escaping

`request.referer` is a request header, and the only validation is that its host matches `SiteSetting.embeddable_host`. Its path/query is interpolated unescaped into a JavaScript string. A referer such as `http://eviltrout.com/';alert(1);//` breaks out of the string and executes in the Discourse iframe, allowing script in the Discourse origin. Escape the value with `escape_javascript`/`to_json` and use a fixed or parsed origin for the `postMessage` target instead of the raw referer.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same XSS vulnerability: request.referer is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, allowing malicious header content to execute arbitrary scripts in the application's context.

false_positives.candidate:
Raw HTML imports bypass sanitization and allow stored XSS

`TopicEmbed.import` stores external feed/article content with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. `Post#cook` returns `raw` unchanged for raw_html, and `app/views/embed/best.html.erb` renders `post.cooked` with `raw`, so Discourse's normal HTML sanitizer is completely bypassed. `PollFeed` also calls `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)`, which can turn escaped `<script>` into an active `<script>` before import. Anyone controlling or compromising the configured feed/article can execute JavaScript in the Discourse origin (and inside the embed iframe). Sanitize imported HTML with the existing allowed-tag/attribute sanitizer before saving, or do not use raw_html for untrusted feed content.

PostCreator is called inside an outer transaction, so jobs are enqueued before commit

`PostCreator.create` is invoked inside `Topic.transaction`. `PostCreator` opens its own transaction but it nests inside this one, so its internal block does not commit before it calls `enqueue_jobs` (process_post, feature_topic_users, etc.). Those Sidekiq jobs may run before the topic/post are committed and fail to find them; if the subsequent `TopicEmbed.create!` fails, for example during a duplicate-URL race, the outer transaction rolls back the post/topic but the already-enqueued jobs remain. Use after_commit callbacks or avoid wrapping PostCreator in an outer transaction.

Embed endpoint enqueues retrieval jobs for arbitrary embed URLs

`best` only checks the request's Referer host; it never checks that `params[:embed_url]` is on the embeddable host before enqueuing `retrieve_topic`. Any non-browser client can forge `Referer: http://<embeddable_host>/` and send unlimited distinct `embed_url`s. The host is rejected later inside `TopicRetriever`, after the Sidekiq job has been accepted, and `invalid_host?` short-circuits before the Redis throttle, so invalid URLs are never throttled. This allows unauthenticated queue flooding, and the loading page reloads every 30 seconds, enqueueing more jobs. Validate the embed URL host and throttle before enqueueing.

PollFeed tests for feed URL and username do not enable polling

In the 'requires feed_polling_url' and 'requires embed_by_username' examples, `feed_polling_enabled?` is left at its default `false`. The `&&` chain stops at that first condition, so `poll_feed` is never called regardless of the URL or username setting, and these tests still pass even if those checks are removed. Stub `feed_polling_enabled?` to true, along with the other required settings, in those examples.

Disqus import now depends on remote fetches and drops the category option

The import task now creates the initial post through `TopicEmbed.import_remote`, which fetches `t[:link]` over the network and returns nil if the fetch fails or the link is not an HTTP URL. In that case the entire thread's comments are skipped, whereas the old code always created a topic from the local XML. The `--category` option was also removed, so existing invocations using it fail and imported threads no longer receive the requested category. Keep a fallback initial post/category or handle the failure explicitly.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Second `self.downsize` definition silently replaces the width/height version and breaks existing callers

The file now defines `self.downsize` twice: line 145 keeps the old signature `(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts = {})` and line 149 adds `(from, to, dimensions, opts = {})`. In Ruby the later definition wins, so the 5-argument form at line 145 is dead code. Any code that still calls the old signature (e.g. `ImageSizer.downsize(from, to, width, height, opts)`, scripts, or plugins that pass width and height) now raises `ArgumentError: wrong number of arguments (5 for 3..4)` on every invocation, so whatever that path did (avatars/attachment/post image downsizing) stops working at runtime. The old arity should be preserved in a single method that accepts either a dimensions string or width+height (e.g. a splat/branch), with a test for both call forms.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify duplicate downsize definitions, with the later dimensions-string signature overriding the original width/height signature and breaking existing callers that pass separate width and height arguments.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side size limit hardcoded to 10MB, ignoring the configured site settings

`maxSizeKB` is now hardcoded to `10 * 1024` instead of reading `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, and the 413 handler at line 246 similarly reports a fabricated 10240 KB maximum. Consequences: (1) admins can no longer constrain what the client lets users select; (2) the same 10MB cap is applied to attachments, which the new server-side downsize logic does not touch, so a multi-megabyte attachment passes client validation and is only rejected (by the still-configured server limit) after the whole body has been uploaded; (3) the displayed `max_size_kb` in error messages no longer matches the actual server/nginx limit. Read the site settings and only relax the cap for images that the server will downsize.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same hardcoded 10 MB client-side limit that ignores per-type site settings, causing divergence from server limits, and also explicitly covers the 413 handler's incorrect reported maximum.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Percentage dimensions passed by the new caller are not valid for the gifsicle (`--resize-fit`) path

The controller calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(from, to, "80%", allow_animation: ...)`. For animated GIFs with `allow_animated_thumbnails` enabled, `optimize` dispatches to `downsize_instructions_animated` -> `resize_instructions_animated`, which emits `gifsicle ... --resize-fit 80%`. `--resize-fit` expects a `WIDTHxHEIGHT` pair (or `--scale 0.8x0.8`), not a percentage, so gifsicle exits non-zero, `convert_with` returns false, the GIF is never shrunk, and (combined with the ignored return value above) the loop burns all five attempts and then stores the oversized file. Pass pixel dimensions for the animated path, or use `--scale`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: passing "80%" for animated GIF downsizing when animated thumbnails are enabled produces an invalid gifsicle --resize-fit argument, which expects WxH geometry, causing downsizing to fail.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsize loop ignores failure and never verifies the result, so oversized images are stored silently

`OptimizedImage.downsize` returns false when ImageMagick/gifsicle fails (corrupt file, unsupported format, missing binaries), and the return value is discarded here. When it fails the temp file is unchanged, so the `while` condition stays true and the identical expensive conversion is executed up to 5 times. When the loop exits, there is no check that the file actually got under `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` (5 passes of 80% may be insufficient for a large image and a small limit), and nothing rejects the upload. The result is that `max_image_size_kb` is silently bypassed for images that cannot be reduced, and up to five image-conversion subprocesses are spent on the request/deferred job for nothing. Break out of the loop when `downsize` returns false and return an error to the user if the final size still exceeds the limit. The guard is also only extension based (`FileHelper.is_image?`), so a non-image file named `*.jpg` triggers the same five doomed conversions.

In-place downsize destroys the original: animated GIFs lose their animation and JPEGs are re-encoded repeatedly

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, ...)` rewrites the upload's temp file in place, i.e. the only copy of the user's file is destructively modified. The non-animated instructions use `convert #{from}[0]`, which selects only the first frame, so with the default `allow_animated_thumbnails` disabled a large animated GIF is replaced by a single static frame and the animation is irrecoverably lost. Iterating the loop also re-encodes the same JPEG up to five times, compounding generation loss. Downsize into a separate temp file, never replace multi-frame GIFs when animation cannot be preserved, and only swap in the result when it is genuinely smaller.

API URL downloads now capped at a hardcoded 10MB instead of `max_image_size_kb`, ignoring configuration in both directions

`FileHelper.download(url, SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes, ...)` became `FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)`. An API client can now make the server fetch and process up to 10MB from an arbitrary URL regardless of the admin's configured image limit (followed by up to five ImageMagick runs per request), which is a resource-amplification change not controlled by any setting. Conversely, if an admin configures `max_image_size_kb` above 10MB, API URL uploads that used to be accepted now fail: `FileHelper.download` returns nil (the `rescue nil`) and the following `tempfile.size` raises `NoMethodError`, returning a 500 instead of a meaningful validation error. The download cap should be derived from the configured limits, not a constant.

Public `OptimizedImage.optimize` arity changed and `OptimizedImage.dimensions` removed without updating callers

`self.optimize` changed from `(operation, from, to, width, height, opts)` to `(operation, from, to, dimensions, opts)`, and the public helper `self.dimensions(width, height)` was deleted. Only three files are touched by this PR, so any other caller (plugins, maintenance scripts, specs) that used either method with the old signature now fails with `ArgumentError`/`NoMethodError`. Either keep backwards-compatible signatures or grep and update every in-repo caller in the same change.

No tests for the new automatic-downsize behaviour or the changed `downsize` signature

The PR adds an untested upload path and an untested change to `OptimizedImage.downsize`, which is why the broken overload and the ignored-failure loop above were not caught. Add specs covering: uploading an image larger than `max_image_size_kb` results in a stored file at or below the limit; an image that cannot be downsized yields an error rather than a silently oversized upload; an animated GIF with `allow_animated_thumbnails` disabled/enabled; and `OptimizedImage.downsize` called both with a dimensions string and with width/height.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unsubscribe can 500 on a missing TopicUser and bypasses notification bookkeeping

The new action does `tu = TopicUser.find_by(...)` and then calls `tu.notification_level` and `tu.save!` without a nil check. A logged-in user who can see the topic but has no TopicUser row (for example a forwarded email link, or a record removed by cleanup) will get a 500 instead of being unsubscribed. Even when the row exists, assigning and saving it directly bypasses TopicUser.change, so notifications_changed_at/notifications_reason_id are not updated and no MessageBus notification_level_change is published; other open tabs keep the old notification state. Use TopicUser.change(current_user.id, params[:topic_id], notification_level: target_level), which creates the row and publishes the change.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same nil-pointer issue: TopicUser.find_by can return nil when no record exists, and calling notification_level or save! without a nil check causes a crash/500. The additional bookkeeping concern does not negate this match.

false_positives.candidate: Per-topic unsubscribe is a CSRF-able GET with no token The new `get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` / `get "t/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` routes perform a state change (notification_level) and rely only on the session cookie. topics_controller skips check_xhr for this action, so non-XHR requests are accepted, and the JSON form `/t/123/unsubscribe.json` bypasses the slug check because `params[:slug].blank?` is only rejected for non-JSON requests. A malicious page can therefore include `` (or many IDs) and silently mute a logged-in victim from topics. Make this a POST with CSRF protection or use a signed per-email token; do not mutate state on an unauthenticated GET.

Unsubscribe is not idempotent; reloading the link mutes further

The action always computes a new level from the current one: watching/tracking goes to regular, then regular goes to muted. Because the unsubscribe URL is a GET, refreshing the confirmation page or opening the same email link again invokes the action again and keeps lowering the level. A user who unsubscribed once from a watched topic and reloads to read the confirmation will be muted. Set a fixed target level (or no-op when the current level is already at/below it) so the operation is idempotent.

Global unsubscribe_link now requires unsubscribe_url from every caller

The shared `unsubscribe_link` translation now unconditionally interpolates `%{unsubscribe_url}`. Email::MessageBuilder calls `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` for every email with `add_unsubscribe_link: true`, but this PR only supplies the new key in UserNotifications#send_notification_email. Any other mailer or plugin using MessageBuilder with `add_unsubscribe_link: true` will raise I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument at send time. Either keep the existing preferences-only fallback or update all callers/make the per-topic sentence conditional.

No test asserts the new per-topic unsubscribe link or controller behavior

The spec change only adds `unsubscribe_url` to the builder so the existing translation does not fail; the assertions still check only the user-preferences URL and the List-Unsubscribe header, never the new per-topic link. There is also no controller/request spec for TopicsController#unsubscribe covering a missing TopicUser, notification-level transitions, the slug redirect, or the JSON/CSRF path. Add assertions for the rendered link and controller specs for those branches.

false_positives.candidate:
deleteCache mutation does not invalidate connectedCalendars query, leaving stale cache UI

It never invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`, so the `cacheUpdatedAt` value that drives the "Cache Status" row and the "Delete cached data" item is not refetched. After a successful delete the dropdown still shows the old timestamp and offers the delete action again until the query happens to refetch. The sibling `disconnectMutation` correctly calls `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate()` in onSettled; the delete-cache path should do the same.

Instantiating CalendarCacheRepository directly bypasses the calendar-cache feature gate

Everywhere else the cache layer is obtained via `CalendarCache.init(...)`, which returns `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` when the `calendar-cache` feature is disabled. Here `new CalendarCacheRepository()` is constructed directly, so `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` always issues a `groupBy` query against `CalendarCache` on every `connectedCalendars` request, even for users/orgs that do not have calendar cache enabled. It also surfaces "cache status" for stale rows left over from when the feature was enabled. Use `CalendarCache.init(null)` so the feature flag is respected.

Cache status ignores expiresAt, reporting expired cache as present

`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` aggregates `_max(updatedAt)` over all rows for the credential, including rows whose `expiresAt` is in the past. `getCachedAvailability` only serves rows with `expiresAt >= now()`, so the UI can show a "Cache Status / Last updated" for data that is already expired and no longer used. The `dev:cron` script was changed from `ts-node cron-tester.ts` to `npx tsx cron-tester.ts`, but `tsx` is not listed in apps/web devDependencies (only `ts-node` is). `npx` will therefore try to download `tsx` on demand, making the script non-reproducible and liable to fail or prompt in offline/CI/restricted environments. New destructive mutation and cache-status query have no tests

`deleteCacheHandler` performs an access-control check (credential must belong to `ctx.user`) and then deletes rows; `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` is a new query used to drive UI. Neither has any unit/integration test. Given this is a destructive, authorization-sensitive endpoint, at minimum there should be a test that a credentialId belonging to another user is rejected and that a valid delete removes exactly that credential's cache rows.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours check uses the slot start time for both `start` and `end`

`const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` is identical to `start`, so the `end > workingHour.endTime` condition only re-tests the start time and can never detect a slot that begins inside the host's working hours but ends after them (e.g. host available until 10:00, 60-minute slot at 09:30). Such slots are then accepted for fixed hosts in round-robin events, allowing a booking outside the fixed host's working hours, which is the situation this change is supposed to prevent. `end` must be derived from the slot end (`slotEndTime`), not the slot start.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the exact same bug: end time is calculated from slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime, causing the working-hours check to miss slots that end outside allowed hours.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs objects compared with `===`, so the zero-length-override check never fires

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` compares object references, not times, and `.add()` returns new Dayjs instances, so this is always false. The intended handling of zero-length (unavailable-day) overrides is therefore dead code, and only the following instant comparisons apply. Use `.isSame(...)` instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: using === to compare Dayjs objects compares references rather than time values, making the comparison false. Both recommend using .isSame() instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Date override short-circuits before the busy check, so already-booked slots are reported available

In `checkIfIsAvailable`, once a slot falls inside a date override the function returns `true` at line 134, before the `busy.every(...)` check at the end of the function. A date override is only meant to replace the working-hours check; the host's `busy` entries (Cal bookings plus connected-calendar events) must still make the slot unavailable. Because personal events mark every user as `isFixed`, and this helper is used for both the fixed-host filter and the loose-host filter, any host with a date override will be shown as available during a time they are already booked, producing bookable slots that double-book the host. The new tests place no booking on the override day, so this is not caught.

`workingHours.find` rejects a slot when any same-day range does not contain it and never rejects a non-working day

The block rejects the slot whenever `workingHours.find(...)` returns a range whose `days` include the weekday and whose bounds do not contain the slot. This has two wrong consequences: (a) if a host has more than one availability range on the same weekday (the `Availability` model/API permits multiple rows for a date), a slot inside range 2 is still rejected because it is outside range 1; (b) if no range exists for that weekday at all (the host does not work that day), nothing matches and the slot is accepted, so a round-robin event still offers slots on days the fixed host is unavailable. The correct test is 'reject unless some range covers the slot', e.g. `workingHours.some(w => w.days.includes(day) && start >= w.startTime && end <= w.endTime)`.

Multiple date overrides on the same day: first non-matching override marks the slot unavailable

`dateOverrides.find(...)` stops as soon as the callback returns `true`, and the callback returns `true` when the override is on the slot's day but the slot is outside that override's range. If a user has two overrides on the same date (e.g. 10:00-11:00 and 14:00-15:00, which the `Availability` table permits), a slot inside the second range is reported as unavailable because it is outside the first. The day should be classified with `some()` - is the slot covered by at least one override on that date - before deciding availability.

Override day match mixes local and UTC dates and only looks at the override start

`dayjs(date.start)` is a Dayjs in the server's local timezone, while `slotStartTime` was created with `.utc()`, so the `format("YYYY MM DD")` comparison compares a local date against a UTC date. On servers not running in UTC (and near day boundaries on any server) the override is attached to the wrong date. In addition, the match uses only the converted `start` instant, so an override whose real-UTC window crosses midnight (typical for early-morning overrides in positive-offset organizer timezones, e.g. 05:00-06:30 Asia/Kolkata) is not recognized for the slots after UTC midnight; those slots then fall through to the working-hours check and are wrongly dropped. Build the override window with `dayjs.utc(...)` and test whether the slot overlaps that window instead of string-comparing dates.

No coverage for the fixed-host round-robin fix or for a booking inside a date override

The added test only asserts the UTC output of `getSlots` for a second invitee timezone. All asserted slots (08:30-12:30 UTC) also lie inside the fixture's normal working hours (04:00-12:30 UTC), so the assertions still pass if the new date-override/working-hours logic in `checkIfIsAvailable` is removed entirely - the test does not exercise the router change. The PR's headline fix (a round-robin event whose fixed host has a date override) has no test, and no test puts an existing booking inside the override window, so the busy-check bypass in `checkIfIsAvailable` is not detected.

Test comment gives the wrong reason for the expected result

The comment `// it should return the same as this is the utc time` is misleading: the invitee gets the same UTC slots in both cases because the slots are absolute instants and the override is anchored to the organizer's timezone, not because 'this is the utc time'. As written it suggests the second assertion is trivially true, whereas it is precisely the assertion that fails with the old `getUTCHours()` logic (which would yield 08:00/09:00/10:00/11:00 UTC for Asia/Dhaka). The comment should explain that the override must represent the same absolute time regardless of the viewer's timezone.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry count uses a stale read-modify-write instead of an atomic increment

Both failure paths write `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` using the value fetched once before the loop. If two cron invocations overlap—there is no locking in this endpoint—or the row is updated by another process, one increment is lost, so the reminder can be retried more times than intended and deletion is delayed or skipped. Use an atomic Prisma update such as `retryCount: { increment: 1 }` (ideally with a claim/conditional update so overlapping runs do not both send).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same stale read-modify-write of retryCount that can lose increments under concurrency, including both failure paths, and recommend Prisma's atomic increment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry cleanup deletes reminders of any method and any scheduled state

The new OR branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` is not constrained by `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` or `scheduled: false`. Because `retryCount` lives on the shared `WorkflowReminder` model, this SMS cron can delete email/WhatsApp reminders, and can also delete a reminder whose SMS has already been scheduled if its retry count ever exceeds 1 (for example through interleaved cron runs). Those rows are then permanently lost, so later cancellation logic cannot find the scheduled reminder. Scope the retry branch to SMS unscheduled reminders, e.g. `{ method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, scheduled: false, retryCount: { gt: 1 } }`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: the retryCount > 1 deletion branch lacks a WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, allowing the SMS scheduler to delete Email and WhatsApp reminders. Its additional concern about scheduled reminders does not change this match.

false_positives.candidate:
Every exception is treated as an SMS send failure and consumes the retry budget

The catch wraps the whole per-reminder flow, not just `twilio.scheduleSMS`. Errors from profile lookup, URL generation, template rendering, or the DB update after Twilio has already accepted the SMS all increment `retryCount`. After two such errors the reminder is deleted. This means transient failures such as a database hiccup or Twilio outage can permanently drop reminders, and a DB update failure after a successful Twilio schedule leaves the row unscheduled so the next run can schedule a duplicate SMS. Only increment for confirmed send failures, and handle post-send persistence errors separately.

Retry update inside catch can abort the whole cron run

The `await prisma.workflowReminder.update(...)` inside `catch` is not itself guarded. If it fails—for example because another cron invocation deleted the row, or the database is unavailable—the error escapes the catch and aborts the handler loop. The remaining unscheduled reminders are then not processed and the endpoint returns an error. The retry bookkeeping should not be able to stop the batch; catch and log failures around it (or use an updateMany and continue).

No tests cover the new retry/deletion behavior

The PR adds a schema column, retry increments on two failure paths, and deletion after the retry limit, but no tests were added. There is no coverage proving that a reminder is kept after one failure, deleted after two failures, that successful scheduling does not get deleted, or that non-SMS reminders are not removed by this SMS cron. These are exactly the failure-sensitive branches where regressions are likely.

Prisma.Sql deep equality fails for reduce-built conditions

These expectations compare a whole Prisma.Sql object with a flat template, but the service builds team/org/filter combinations with nested Prisma.sql calls and reduce. Prisma.Sql equality is structural over its strings and values arrays; nested composition leaves different string segmentation even when the SQL text is identical. For example, the service OR condition has five strings while this flat template has three. Therefore the team, org, and combined-filter assertions at lines 296, 332, and 429 will fail. Compare conditions.sql/text plus values instead, or build the expected SQL with the same nested structure.

getBaseConditions can return an unparenthesized OR expression

When there is no filter, getBaseConditions returns the authorization expression directly. For org/team scopes that expression is an unparenthesized top-level OR, e.g. (A) OR (B). Any caller that composes it as WHERE ${baseConditions} AND ... gets SQL precedence A OR (B AND ...), so the extra predicate is applied only to one branch. This can return rows outside the requested date/status/team range. The returned expression should always be wrapped in parentheses, or callers should use a service method that composes safely.

Public findMany API removed without caller migration

The public findMany method is removed and replaced by getBaseConditions, which only returns a SQL fragment. No caller updates are included in this PR. Any existing consumer of service.findMany(...) will fail to compile or run, and responsibility for applying authorization moves to every raw-query caller; forgetting to interpolate getBaseConditions would query all rows. Keep a query method that applies the conditions, or migrate all callers in the same PR.

Team scope no longer requires teamId at compile time

The new public options type makes teamId optional for every scope, whereas the old constructor type was a discriminated union that required teamId for scope "team". Missing teamId now passes TypeScript, fails the runtime schema, and is silently converted to this.options = null, so the service returns 1=0 (empty results) instead of reporting a configuration error. Retain the discriminated union or throw on validation failure.

Salesforce token refresh references prisma without importing it

HubSpot API calls fail and the stored credential is corrupted whenever sync is enabled.

Zoho Bigin treats a fetch Response as an axios response

In credential-sharing mode `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a fetch `Response`, which has no `.data` property. This line accesses `tokenInfo.data.error`, so refresh throws a TypeError and no token is stored. The local axios path works only when sharing is disabled.

Zoho CRM treats a fetch Response as an axios response

In credential-sharing mode `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a fetch `Response`, not an axios response. `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data` is undefined here, so `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error` throws and Zoho CRM token refresh fails whenever credential sync is enabled.

APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED stores the encryption key instead of a boolean

`process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` returns the encryption key string when both env vars are set. The exported constant is therefore a secret, not an enabled flag. If it is logged, serialized, or imported into code that reaches the client, `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` can leak. Use `Boolean(...)` and keep the key out of exported constants.

Credential-mutating webhook accepts any HTTP method

The handler never checks `req.method`; it will process GET, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE requests as long as the secret header and body are present. A credential-mutating webhook should accept only POST and return 405 for other methods.

Updating synced credentials leaves the invalid flag set

When a credential already exists, the update only changes `key`. If that credential was previously marked `invalid` after a refresh failure, it stays invalid and Cal.com will continue ignoring the fresh credentials from the app store. Synced credentials should reset `invalid` to false.

Salesforce bypasses the configured credential sync endpoint

Unlike the other integrations changed in this PR, Salesforce never calls `refreshOAuthTokens`; it always fetches directly from `login.salesforce.com` using local consumer keys. Consequently, when a self-hoster configures `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` and expects their app store to be the source of truth, Salesforce token refreshes still use Cal.com's local app secrets and never contact the app store.

No tests cover the new credential webhook or token-sharing helpers

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, a process detected as dead/hung is only killed when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. When `produce_to_pipe` is set (the code uses `threading.Thread` instead of a spawn process, as done by the tests), the old thread is neither stopped nor joined before `_create_process_for_shards` overwrites `self.processes[process_index]` with a brand-new thread. Both threads then run `SpanFlusher.main` for the same shards concurrently, producing the same flushed segments twice and racing on `done_flush_segments`/Redis key deletion. This is limited to the thread path, but that path is what the test suite relies on, and a hang-triggered restart there would corrupt results.

Non-positive `max_processes` silently disables the flusher or spawns one process per shard

`self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` (and `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(...))`) does no validation. Passing `--flusher-processes 0` is treated as falsy and becomes `len(assigned_shards)` (i.e. 'max 0' spawns one process per shard), while a negative value makes `num_processes = min(negative, n)` negative, so `range(self.num_processes)` is empty, `process_to_shards_map`/`processes`/`buffers` are all empty, and no flusher worker is ever created. In that state `submit()` still inserts spans into Redis and forwards to `next_step`, but nothing ever calls `flush_segments`, so segments are never expired or produced and Redis grows without bound — with no error or warning. Validate that `max_processes >= 1` (or explicitly define the meaning of 0) rather than relying on `or`.

`_create_process_for_shard` is dead code and never called

`_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is defined but no caller exists; the restart path in `_ensure_processes_alive` calls `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly. This unused method adds confusion about whether a single-shard restart path is supposed to exist (it would also break the assumption that a process owns a fixed set of shards) and should be removed.

New multiprocess flusher is only checked structurally, not for actual flushing or restart behavior

test_flusher_processes_limit only asserts the sizes of `processes`/`process_to_shards_map` and then calls `step.join()`; it runs in thread mode (`produce_to_pipe`) and never submits spans, so it never verifies that spans for different partitions are actually flushed/produced by the correct per-shard processes, nor does it exercise `_ensure_processes_alive` (dead/hung restart) or the per-process backpressure accounting. The core new behavior (each process flushing its own shards and restarting independently) has no functional test coverage.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

Error details can be paired with the wrong replay error IDs

true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same issue as the golden comment: zip(error_ids, events.values()) misaligns IDs because dict ordering isn't guaranteed and missing nodes shift the pairing.
